summary_html: Agency fails to **disclose required data or reports**, obstructing transparency. Federal statutes require public reporting under CAPTA, FOIA, and Sunshine provisions.
authority_html:
- **CAPTA (42 U.S.C. §§ 5101–5116)** — mandates public availability of child-fatality information  
- **Freedom of Information Act (5 U.S.C. § 552)** — public access to federal records  
- **Government in the Sunshine Act (5 U.S.C. § 552b)** — open-meeting requirements

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: Vining v. Council of the District of Columbia
key_cases.court: District of Columbia Court of Appeals
key_cases.holding: The Council may not invoke the Legislative Privilege Act through D.C. FOIA Exemption 6 (or, on this record, Exemption 4) to withhold documents responsive to a FOIA request, and summary judgment for the Council was reversed.
key_cases.relevance: It is the D.C. decision rejecting a public body's attempt to expand a FOIA exemption to defeat disclosure.
key_cases.quote: We conclude that the Legislative Privilege Act cannot be invoked through Exemption 6 so as to permit the Council to withhold documents responsive to a FOIA request

key_cases.case_name: District of Columbia v. Fraternal Order of Police, Metropolitan Police Department Labor Committee
key_cases.court: District of Columbia Court of Appeals
key_cases.holding: Under D.C. FOIA's personal privacy exemption the negligible public interest in the identities of employees who sent emails under a pledge of confidentiality did not outweigh their privacy interest, so the District was entitled to withhold the identifying information.
key_cases.relevance: It defines the personal privacy limit on what a requester can compel a District agency to disclose.
key_cases.quote: we conclude that FOIA does not require the District of Columbia to disclose the identities of the email authors

key_cases.case_name: V.K. v. Child & Family Services Agency
key_cases.court: District of Columbia Court of Appeals
key_cases.holding: On judicial review of a CFSA administrative decision upholding a 'substantiated' abuse entry in the Child Protection Register, CFSA bears the burden by a preponderance at the fair hearing and the court will disturb the hearing officer's finding only if the record compels a contrary conclusion; the decision was affirmed on substantial evidence.
key_cases.relevance: It sets out the confidentiality and expungement rules governing the Child Protection Register.
key_cases.quote: At the hearing, CFSA bore the burden of proof by a preponderance of the evidence.
